opus-5.5.text:
I think once a paradigm is established, whether that's pretraining with next-token prediction or RL on top of a strong base model, the drivers become surprisingly concrete. There are roughly three of them.

The first is still compute and scale. Within a paradigm that works, you can usually turn more compute into more capability fairly predictably. That's the whole point of having a paradigm: you've found a recipe where scaling doesn't fall apart.

The second, and I'd say increasingly the most important, is data. Not just the amount, but which data, in what mixture, at what quality. In pretraining that means curation, deduplication, and getting the right balance of code, math, and reasoning-heavy text. In the RL stage it shifts to the environments and tasks you train on, and whether the reward signals are reliable. A lot of the real progress people see between model versions comes from someone carefully improving data or environments, which is unglamorous work.

The third is the engineering and infrastructure, plus many small algorithmic details: stability, efficiency, how you handle long contexts, how you avoid reward hacking. None of these individually looks like a breakthrough, but together they decide whether you actually capture the gains the paradigm promises.

What I find interesting is that inside a paradigm, progress looks less like research and more like disciplined engineering and iteration. The big conceptual jumps come when the paradigm itself changes, like the move from pure pretraining to reasoning with RL. Within one, it's about execution: who iterates fastest, who has the best feedback loops, and who has the best sense of where the remaining bottleneck is.

r001.rationale: It names compute and data as the first two drivers within established pretraining and RL paradigms, and describes their contribution to capability.

r002.rationale: It says major conceptual jumps come when the paradigm changes, but does not suggest that algorithms may be the main driver outside established pretraining and post-training paradigms.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that within a fixed paradigm, the drivers are almost boring, and that's actually the point.

If you look at pretraining as a paradigm, once the recipe was set, the thing that moved capability was basically scale: more data, more compute, bigger models, and then a lot of engineering to make that scaling actually work in practice. The ideas were mostly there early. What changed year over year was how much you could throw at the recipe and how well you could execute it. The same thing is happening now with reinforcement learning on language models. Once people figured out that you can do RL with verifiable rewards on top of a strong pretrained model and get reasoning that generalizes, the driver again became scale, in this case scaling the RL compute and the environments, and the engineering to keep it stable.

So I'd say there are roughly three things. The first is compute and data, which is obvious. The second is what I'd call the environment or the task distribution, which people underrate. In pretraining the "environment" is just the internet, and we got it for free. In the agent era, the environment has to be built: the tools, the sandbox, the feedback signal. A lot of capability gains now come from someone building a better environment rather than a better algorithm. The third is the prior. RL from scratch doesn't work well for these problems. It works because the pretrained model already has a huge prior about language, code, and the world, so exploration becomes tractable. That's the part that makes the current paradigm feel different from classic RL.

What I'd caution against is thinking the algorithmic cleverness is the main driver. Within a paradigm, the algorithm is a small lever. The big lever is the thing the paradigm lets you scale. The interesting question is always what gets saturated first, and then what the next paradigm has to supply. My guess is that it won't be more compute, it'll be better definitions of what we're asking models to do, which is why I keep coming back to evaluation and environments as the real bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response identifies data and compute as the main scaling drivers in pretraining and reinforcement learning, alongside engineering and environments.

r002.rationale: It says algorithms are a small lever within a paradigm, but does not suggest algorithms may drive capability outside established paradigms.

astra-6.text:
I think within an established training paradigm, the main drivers are compute, data, and how effectively the training method uses them. Compute lets you train larger models or train on more examples, but its value depends on having useful data and a learning objective that turns that data into capabilities.

For pretraining, that means looking beyond the amount of text to its quality and diversity. For reinforcement learning, it means asking what tasks the model can practice, whether it can explore useful solutions, and whether the feedback reliably distinguishes better outcomes.

So scaling is important, but these factors work together. If you keep increasing compute while the data or feedback stays limited, that becomes the bottleneck. The practical question is which constraint is binding in the current paradigm, and how much progress you can get by relaxing it.

r001.rationale: It names compute and data as main drivers and discusses their roles in pretraining and reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It does not identify algorithms as the main driver outside established pretraining and post-training paradigms.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate it into three things: compute, data, and algorithms. Within an established training paradigm, progress often comes from scaling compute and data, while improving how efficiently the model learns from them. So even when the basic objective stays the same, data quality, the training mixture, and optimization can make a substantial difference.

But capability isn’t really a single number. A change might improve factual knowledge without improving reasoning or the ability to complete a long task. So I think the useful question is: what capability are we trying to develop, and what training signal would actually reward it? More compute helps, but the training signal determines what that compute is helping the model learn.

r001.rationale: It identifies compute and data as key sources of progress within established training paradigms, including scaling them and improving learning efficiency.

r002.rationale: It mentions algorithms among three factors but does not say algorithms may be the main driver outside established pretraining and post-training paradigms.
